Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 61, verse 1–4:

(p-249) Surat al-Saff

It is also called Surat al-Hawariyyin (the Surah of the Disciples).

There are two opinions about it.

The first: it is Madaniyyah (revealed in Madinah). This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Qatadah, and the majority.

The second: it is Makkiyyah (revealed in Makkah). This was said by Ibn Yasar.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are five opinions.

The first: what Abu Salamah narrated from ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, who said: "A group of us companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sat together, and we said: 'If we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, we would perform them.' So Allah revealed ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth exalts Allah﴾ to the end of the surah."

(p-250) The second: "A man would come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and say: 'I did such-and-such,' when he had not done it, so ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ was revealed." This was narrated by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas. Likewise al-Dahhak said: a man would say, "I fought," when he had not fought; "I thrust a spear," when he had not thrust; "I was patient," when he had not been patient. So this verse was revealed.

The third: some Muslims used to say before jihad was prescribed: "We wish that Allah, Exalted is He, would show us the deeds most beloved to Him." Then when jihad was legislated, some of the believers disliked it, so this verse was revealed. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: Suhayb killed a man on the day of Badr. Then a man came and claimed that he had killed him and took his spoils. Suhayb said: "I killed him, O Messenger of Allah." So the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that the spoils be handed over to Suhayb, and this verse was revealed. This was narrated by Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib from Suhayb.

The fifth: the hypocrites used to say to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions: "If you go out, we will go out with you and support you." But when the Prophet (ﷺ) went out, they turned back from him, so this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

(p-251) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿maqtan﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and the meaning is: "Your saying what you do not do is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed what He loves, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row, as if they were a solid structure﴾, meaning: a structure whose parts are joined to one another. Thus He informed that He loves whoever stands firm in jihad and remains in his place, like the firmness of a solid structure. It is also possible that He meant that their steadfastness in fighting their enemy should be equal, so that they are, in unity of word, like a solid structure. The exegetes have two opinions about the meaning of "marsus" (solid):

The first: it is that which is joined part to part, so no flaw is seen in it due to its solidity. This was said by most of them.

The second: it is that which is built with lead, and al-Farra' went in this direction. Abu Bahriyyah (p-252) used to say: "They disliked fighting on horseback and preferred fighting on foot, due to this verse."

The name of Abu Bahriyyah: ʿAbdullah ibn Qays al-Targhami; he narrated from Muʿadh. It seems he indicated by this that horsemen generally do not line up in formation; rather, infantry does.

The Almighty's words: ﴿When they deviated﴾, meaning they inclined away from the truth. ﴿God caused their hearts to deviate﴾, meaning He turned their hearts away from the truth as a recompense for what they had committed. What follows is clear up to His words ﴿[a messenger] who will come after me﴾.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read مِن بَعْدِيَ اسْمُهُ (*min ba'di yasmuhu*, "after me, whose name is") with a fatha on the ya' (the final yā' of بَعْدِي is vocalized, making it *min ba'diya*). Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read مِن بَعْدِي اسْمُهُ with the ya' sukun (*min ba'di*, the yā' unvocalized).

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God﴾. There are two opinions regarding them:

The first: they are the Jews. This is the view of Muqatil.

The second: they are the Christians, when they said, "'Isa is the son of God." This is the view of Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Ibn Mas'ud, 'Asim al-Jahdari, and Talhah ibn Musarrif read يَدَّعِي إلى الإسْلامِ (*yaddā'ī ila al-Islām*, "is called to Islam") with a fatha on the ya' and the dal, with the dal shaddah, and with a kasra on the 'ayn.

What follows, in [Surah al-Tawbah: 32], up to His words ﴿perfecting His light﴾: Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, and Khalaf read مُتِمُّ نُورِهِ (*mutimmu nūrihi*) as an idafah (construct phrase, with the noun in the genitive). Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read مُتِمٌّ (*mutimmun*) in the nominative with tanwin.

(p-254) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Shall I direct you to a transaction?﴾ The exegetes (mufassirun) said: This verse was revealed when they said, "If we knew which deeds are most beloved to God, we would perform them forever." So God directed them to that and made it like a trade because of the profit they would gain from it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿will save you﴾ (tunjikum). Ibn 'Amir read *tunajjikum* with the doubled letter (tashdid), and the rest read it without doubling (takhfif). Then He explained the trade, saying, the Exalted: ﴿You believe in God﴾ up to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He will forgive you﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿He will forgive you﴾ is the answer (jawab) to His saying *tu'minun* ("you believe") and *wa tujahidun* ("and you strive"), because its meaning is the meaning of a command. The meaning is: Believe in God and strive, and He will forgive you; that is, if you do that, He will forgive you. Some grammarians erred and said: This is the answer to "Shall I direct you?" This is a clear error, because it is not the case that when He directs them to what benefits them they are forgiven; rather they are forgiven only when they act upon it. As for the one who reads *yaghfir lakum* with the assimilation of the *ra'* into the *lam* (idgham, the merging of one letter into the next), this is not permissible according to Sibawayh and al-Khalil, because the *ra'* is not assimilated into the *lam* in such constructions. (p-255) It has been transmitted from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', and he is a great imam; I do not think he read it except that he had heard it from the Arabs. Sibawayh, al-Khalil and all the Basran grammarians, except Abu 'Amr, claimed that the *lam* is assimilated into the *ra'*, but the *ra'* is not assimilated into the *lam*. Their argument is that the *ra'* is a strong, repeated letter, so if it were assimilated into the *lam*, its repetition would be lost. What follows this has already been mentioned up to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and another [blessing] you love﴾. Al-Farra' said: The meaning is: For you, in this world along with the reward of the Hereafter, there is another [blessing] you love, and then He explained it by saying, the Exalted: ﴿help from God and a near victory﴾. On this there are two opinions:

One: It is the conquest of Makkah; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: It is the conquest of Persia and Rome; this was said by 'Ata'.
